notes: Replaced bootstrap-credential-retirement with shared-bootstrap-discovery-forgery and node-firewall-supplements-pod-isolation with node-firewall-kubelet-control-plane-path to test specific security consequences instead of general hardening advice.

cards.statement: A kubelet with anonymous authentication disabled directly rejects unauthenticated HTTPS requests.
cards.explanation: The kubelet returns 401 Unauthorized when a caller fails authentication and anonymous access is disabled.

cards.statement: A kubelet using client certificate authentication enforces Kubernetes RBAC permissions by default.
cards.explanation: Client certificates establish identity. A kubelet's default authorization allows authenticated requests; Webhook authorization delegates permission checks to the API server.
cards.misconception: Kubelet certificate authentication automatically activates RBAC authorization.

cards.statement: A kubelet with token webhook authentication validates a presented ServiceAccount token through the API server.
cards.explanation: The kubelet sends a TokenReview to its configured API server, so bearer-token identity checks use that server's authentication.

cards.statement: The API server verifies the kubelet's serving certificate on its default HTTPS connection to that kubelet.
cards.explanation: The API server's default kubelet connection skips serving-certificate verification. Configuring a trusted kubelet CA bundle closes this server-identity gap.
cards.misconception: HTTPS automatically verifies the kubelet's server identity.

source.title: Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane

cards.statement: With kubelet Webhook authorization, a caller's get on nodes/proxy permits container command execution.
cards.explanation: Some kubelet command endpoints accept WebSocket GET requests. Their authorization uses get, making nodes/proxy access more powerful than read access.

cards.statement: Kubernetes admission controllers validate container commands sent directly to a kubelet's HTTPS endpoint.
cards.explanation: Commands sent directly to the kubelet bypass Kubernetes admission. Restrict this separate endpoint to preserve the cluster's security boundary.
cards.misconception: API server admission also covers direct kubelet commands.

cards.statement: With authorization disabled, etcd accepts data writes from a client using a trusted health-check certificate.
cards.explanation: Client-certificate authentication alone gives a trusted etcd client broad data access; a certificate's health-check purpose supplies no restriction.

cards.statement: Kubernetes RBAC limits the objects a client may modify through a direct connection to the etcd API.
cards.explanation: Direct etcd clients bypass Kubernetes RBAC. Kubernetes API permissions do not restrict this separate data-access route.
cards.misconception: Direct etcd requests inherit Kubernetes RBAC permissions.

cards.statement: For a CNI enforcement flaw, kubeadm leaves the provider's security update separate from control plane upgrades.
cards.explanation: kubeadm leaves CNI provider upgrades to operators. A provider's fix for vulnerable networking code follows that project's upgrade instructions.

cards.statement: A kubeadm control plane upgrade installs the kubelet patch for a worker-node kubelet vulnerability.
cards.explanation: A kubelet security fix has to reach the affected node's kubelet binary. The control plane upgrade leaves that installation to the operator.
cards.misconception: A control plane upgrade also patches worker kubelet binaries.

cards.statement: Container-focused node operating systems reduce the host attack surface exposed by a container escape.
cards.explanation: These node operating systems isolate system components and provide essential container services, reducing host services an escaped process can target.

cards.statement: Running a container as an unprivileged user prevents network protocol kernel module autoload.
cards.explanation: Unprivileged processes can trigger some protocol modules by opening suitable sockets. Remove or block unused modules on Kubernetes nodes.
cards.misconception: An unprivileged container cannot trigger kernel module loading.

cards.statement: Write access to a kubelet's configured static Pod manifests gives a user a path to launch local workloads.
cards.explanation: The kubelet watches its configured manifest directory and starts Pods from added files. Protecting writes to that source protects local workload creation.

cards.statement: A user with a node's container runtime socket access can launch containers outside Kubernetes RBAC.
cards.explanation: The runtime accepts local commands through its socket. Its filesystem access controls protect this route to container creation.

cards.statement: An admission rule blocking a runtime socket's exact path can leave access through a parent hostPath mount.
cards.explanation: Restricting the socket's exact path is insufficient when a workload receives a hostPath mount that includes its parent directory.

cards.statement: A Pod's read-only hostPath mount protects mounted kubelet credentials from disclosure to the Pod.
cards.explanation: Read-only hostPath access still exposes readable host files. A workload can steal privileged kubelet credentials through such a mount.
cards.misconception: Read-only hostPath access also protects file confidentiality.

cards.statement: A bootstrap token holder can forge cluster-info signatures for another client using the same token.
cards.explanation: Bootstrap discovery uses the token as a shared signing secret. A client that knows it can create a valid discovery signature, so sharing one token across clients weakens this trust boundary.

cards.statement: On a swap-enabled node where kubelet detects unsupported noswap, Secret volume backing confines credentials to RAM.
cards.explanation: When the kernel rejects noswap, the kubelet warns and continues. Secret volume tmpfs contents can then reach persistent swap storage.
cards.misconception: Memory-backed Secret volumes stay off persistent storage under swap.

cards.statement: kubectl treats an untrusted kubeconfig as inert data when accessing a Kubernetes cluster.
cards.explanation: A crafted kubeconfig can execute malicious code on kubectl's host. Inspect configurations from untrusted sources before use.
cards.misconception: A kubeconfig cannot execute code or expose files on its consumer's host.

source.title: Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files

cards.statement: An admission allowlist confines an untrusted Pod to its approved read-write hostPath directory.
cards.explanation: Directory allowlisting needs read-only hostPath mounts to preserve the intended boundary; an untrusted writer can subvert a writable mount.
cards.misconception: Admission directory allowlisting securely confines read-write hostPath access.

cards.statement: With direct API server-to-kubelet networking, a node firewall blocking that path breaks kubectl logs.
cards.explanation: The API server retrieves Pod logs through the kubelet's HTTPS endpoint. Node firewall rules need to preserve this control-plane path for log requests to succeed.

source.title: Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane

cards.statement: A loaded AppArmor profile in complain mode reports attempted access outside its allow rules.
cards.explanation: AppArmor complain mode reports profile violations for review; it does not turn those reports into an enforcing access policy.

source.title: Linux kernel security constraints for Pods and containers

cards.statement: When its requested Localhost AppArmor profile is missing, kubelet can start a Pod with RuntimeDefault.
cards.explanation: A Pod requesting a Localhost AppArmor profile fails to start when that profile is unavailable on its node. Kubernetes does not substitute RuntimeDefault.
cards.misconception: Kubernetes falls back to RuntimeDefault when a requested local AppArmor profile is unavailable.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Access to Resources with AppArmor

cards.statement: The default scheduler can place an AppArmor-constrained Pod using its inventory of loaded node profiles.
cards.explanation: The scheduler does not track loaded AppArmor profiles. Administrators can use node labels and placement constraints to select nodes prepared for the workload.
cards.misconception: The scheduler discovers which AppArmor profiles each node has loaded.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Access to Resources with AppArmor

cards.statement: An investigator can prove a container's root-process AppArmor profile using the node's loaded-profile list alone.
cards.explanation: A node's list shows available profiles. Inspect /proc/1/attr/current inside the container to establish the AppArmor profile attached to its root process.
cards.misconception: Loading an AppArmor profile establishes that a particular container process uses it.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Access to Resources with AppArmor

cards.statement: The seccomp SCMP_ACT_LOG action permits a matching syscall through its filter while recording it.
cards.explanation: SCMP_ACT_LOG records a syscall and permits execution. That action supplies observations for building a restrictive profile.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

cards.statement: An attacker can exploit a kernel vulnerability through a syscall permitted by a container's seccomp profile.
cards.explanation: Permitted syscalls remain available to an attacker, including paths to vulnerable kernel behavior. seccomp reduces exposure rather than validating those code paths.

source.title: Linux kernel security constraints for Pods and containers

cards.statement: The runtime retains a configured seccompProfile when it starts a container with privileged: true.
cards.explanation: Privileged containers run with seccomp Unconfined. An explicit profile in the workload specification does not keep syscall filtering active.
cards.misconception: An explicit seccompProfile remains effective when the container runs privileged.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

cards.statement: A seccomp allowlist derived from one application release establishes compatibility with a later release.
cards.explanation: An application update may introduce needed syscalls outside a previous allowlist. Test the updated workload against its seccomp profile.
cards.misconception: A seccomp profile proven compatible with one application release also validates later releases.

source.title: Linux kernel security constraints for Pods and containers

cards.statement: RuntimeDefault seccomp profiles can impose different restrictions across container runtimes and their releases.
cards.explanation: RuntimeDefault uses the node runtime's profile. Different runtimes or runtime releases may therefore permit different syscall sets.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

cards.statement: With Pod Security Admission enabled, a namespace's Restricted warn mode rejects a Pod that violates its policy.
cards.explanation: Pod Security Admission's Restricted warn mode returns a user-facing warning and permits the policy violation through that check.
cards.misconception: Warn mode rejects violating Pods instead of permitting them with a warning.

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission lets a namespace enforce Baseline while using Restricted checks in its warn mode.
cards.explanation: Pod Security Admission uses independent mode-level labels. Operators can check a stricter target in warn mode while enforcing a compatible level.

source.title: Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission can supply secure field defaults to a Pod before applying a namespace's Restricted policy.
cards.explanation: Pod Security Admission validates submitted Pods rather than setting security fields. Supply required values in the workload or a separate mutating admission step.
cards.misconception: Pod Security Admission sets secure defaults as part of its validation.

source.title: Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy to the Built-In PodSecurity Admission Controller

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission preserves a namespace's v1.35 checks across upgrades when enforce-version stays v1.35.
cards.explanation: A Pod Security Admission version label fixes a mode's checks to that Kubernetes minor's policy instead of following the latest policy.

source.title: Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission rejects a Deployment whose template violates its namespace's Restricted enforce policy.
cards.explanation: Pod Security Admission's enforce mode checks Pods created from a Deployment, rather than the Deployment request. Workload templates receive audit and warning checks.
cards.misconception: Enforce mode rejects workload templates at Deployment admission.

cards.statement: Pod Security Admission exempts Deployment Pods created by a ReplicaSet controller using an exempt ServiceAccount.
cards.explanation: The ReplicaSet controller submits Pod creation using its own identity. Exempting that account extends the Pod Security Admission bypass to other users' workloads.

cards.statement: A user with unrestricted namespace patch access can weaken that namespace's labeled Pod Security Admission enforcement.
cards.explanation: Changing namespace labels can relax Pod Security Admission's policy level. Reserve namespace update rights for trusted users.

source.title: Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy to the Built-In PodSecurity Admission Controller

cards.statement: In a namespace enforcing Baseline v1.35, Pod Security Admission rejects a nonexempt Pod with a nonempty HTTP probe host.
cards.explanation: The Baseline policy includes the probe host restriction introduced in v1.34. An HTTP probe's host field has to be empty or omitted.

cards.statement: A Linux Pod can pass Restricted admission with Pod and container seccompProfile omitted if its node uses seccompDefault.
cards.explanation: Restricted Pod Security Admission requires an explicit RuntimeDefault or Localhost seccomp profile at Pod or container level. Node runtime defaulting leaves the required API field absent.
cards.misconception: Node seccomp runtime defaults satisfy Restricted admission's explicit-profile requirement.

cards.statement: After a namespace switches to Restricted enforce mode, Pod Security Admission evicts its running violating Pods.
cards.explanation: Changing a namespace's enforce label checks existing Pods and reports violations as warnings. Pod Security Admission leaves those running Pods in place.
cards.misconception: Strengthening an enforce policy evicts existing noncompliant Pods.

source.title: Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels
